newsitem.title: USA: Women urged to use condoms, hormonal contraception.
newsitem.headline: Women urged to use condoms, hormonal contraception.

text.p: Women whose partners use condoms to prevent AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases should not stop taking birth control pills to prevent pregnancy, federal health officials said on Thursday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said a study in five cities found women could be persuaded the combination of hormonal contraceptives and condoms maximized their protection against pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases such as AIDS.

While condoms were the most effective way of reducing the transmission of disease, the CDC said hormonal contraceptives were the best other than sterilization to prevent pregnancy. Hormonal contraceptives can be oral, injected or implanted.

"Hormonal contraceptives and surgical sterilization are more effective at preventing pregnancy, but these methods do not prevent women from acquiring sexually transmitted diseases," CDC epidemiologist Jean Lawrence said.

A study at inner-city clinics in Long Beach, California; San Francisco, Denver, Baltimore and Newark found that the proportion of 1,173 sexually-active women who consistently used condoms rose from 13 percent before AIDS counseling to 36 percent afterwards.

"For women who were using hormonal contraceptives, their consistent condom use increased from 10 percent when they enrolled in the study to about 31 percent three months after the intervention," Lawrence said.

"This is important because in the past we've found that women who use hormonal contraceptives are not as likely to use condoms for HIV and sexually transmitted disease prevention. And we found that we could increase their use with this intervention," she said.

AIDS counseling increased condom usage among women who had undergone tubal ligation or who were medically infertile. Condom use also rose among women who had previously used no contraception, or used minimally effective techniques such as the rhythm method or withdrawal.

"The most common way that women acquire HIV in the United States and throughout the world is by heterosexual contact," Lawrence said. "Therefore, it's important to develop effective strategies to reduce their risk of HIV infection."
